newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Desperate squatters wait for ships out of Albania.
newsitem.headline: Desperate squatters wait for ships out of Albania.

text.p: Hundreds of filthy, unshaven men stinking of body odour sprawl sleeping on rubbish-strewn mounds of grass in the rail yard outside Albania's main port.
They are not drunks sleeping off a binge but would-be refugees waiting for a ship to dock in Durres and carry them away from Albania's chaos to Italy.
The men are exhausted from a night spent huddled around campfires. The first touch of morning sun glinting off the Adriatic provided the warmth necessary for them to finally fall asleep.
Entire families are living rough among the rusted boxcars, broken glass and junked automobiles.

"I sleep with my two children and my husband on bits of cardboard. We have a few blankets but it is still very cold at night," said Parashqevi Flamuri, 38, who has been living in the squatter's camp outside the port for five days.

"Food and water are my biggest worries. The people living here watch out for each other and some of the people from Durres are helping us too. But we haven't seen the Red Cross or the United Nations. I think the world has forgotten us."

About 1,000 people are still living rough outside the port of Durres, Albania's largest. Two or three times that number were here a few days ago but most have drifted off after losing hope of ever catching a ship from here.
Police guarding the port say they fired into the air to drive a ship away at midnight last night after it tried to dock to pick up passengers.
Small craft are picking up paying passengers from beaches along the coast and ferrying them to rusting coasters for the journey to Italy.
The people camped under the watchful eyes of police patrolling the port are the poorest of the poor, unable to afford the several hundred dollars that passage from a beach would cost.

Like many in Albania, they lost what little they had in the recent collapse of five investment schemes, a financial scandal which precipitated widespread civil unrest across Albania, especially in the south.
Flamuri's wife said that neither she or her husband had been able to find work in their hometown of Kavaje, about 30 kms (19 miles) south of Durres, for the past several years.

"We lived on a little money every month from the government. Then we sold our flat to get money for the investment companies, so now we have no home. I would sell my children to get out of this country," the woman said.
Police in Durres say there have been no clashes with the squatters since Sunday but many of the people still in the camp seem determined to stay on.
"We tell them there is no chance they will get a ship but they don't believe us. They are not very smart," said Valentin Hidra, a port policeman.

"What I don't understand is why the countries of Europe won't give our people visas. That's the problem. Albanians have their own culture and identity and some people still have money. We're being discriminated against."

The majority of those living in the squatters camp are young men from the south, lacking education and without much patience for the police or the government, whom they view as harsh, corrupt overlords.
"I was attending a school where the government didn't even provide us with books for our lessons," complained one 18-year squatter named Shkelqim.
"The government is behind this mess. It stole the people's money and let us steal the army's guns so we would begin to kill one another. Our only hope is to escape."
The young man pulled a small handful of sunflower seeds from a trouser pocket and viewed them without appetite. "Look, this is my breakfast. I'm living now like a bird," he said.
